newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone coup leaders win rebel support.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone coup leaders win rebel support.

text.p: Sierra Leone rebel leader Foday Sankoh on Wednesday called on his forces to back the leaders of a weekend coup who are under heavy Nigerian pressure to restore the civilian president.

Nigeria landed 720 troops at Freetown's port and airport on Tuesday to reinforce the 900 already stationed in the country, and a member of the new ruling council said Nigerian defence chiefs were expected later in the day to discuss restoring Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, who fled to Guinea on Sunday.

Freetown's new strongman Major Johnny Paul Koromah said on Tuesday night that Sankoh had agreed to join his government and work for a lasting peace in the war with his Revolutionary United Front (RUF) which began in 1991.

"All RUF field commanders and troops should stand by for any reinforcement needed by Major Koromah to defend our sovereignty," Sankoh, who is currently held at a hotel in the Nigerian capital, said in a broadcast on Sierra Leone state radio.
"The politicians are our enemies, not the army."
Speaking later to Reuters in Lagos by telephone, Sankoh added: "As long as the new government is for peace I am with them. The RUF and the army are now united"
On Monday he had declined to comment on the invitation to join the government but on Wednesday he was emphatic that he wanted to go home and join the new administration.

"I am appealing to the (Nigerian) head of state General Sani Abacha and the people of Nigeria to be neutral. I am appealing to them to let me go and join the armed forced to bring peace to Sierra Leone," he said. Nigeria, the regional power, has so
far not made any public comment on Sankoh's stay in the country, neither has it said anything on the latest coup in Sierra Leone.

A senior military source in Freetown said the Nigerians, who were drawn into combat during the coup on Sunday, were demanding to deploy to protect key installations such as the radio, television and presidential offices.

The Sierra Leone army rulers banned a demonstration called by civilian opponents of the coup for later on Wednesday to demand the return of Kabbah, whose civilian government was elected last March after four years of military rule.

"In consideration of the present security situation in the country, particularly in the capital city, Freetown, government will not permit holding of such demonstrations, public meetings, and processions until further notice," a statement said.
Koromah announced a ban on political parties and suspension of the civilian constitution.
Shops, offices and schools were closed, but schoolchildren headed for examination centres hoping to sit examinations cancelled on Tuesday.
Shooting could be heard in Freetown overnight, and protests against the coup have been reported from towns in the interior.

The military source said senior figures from Nigeria's military government were expected in Freetown later in the day for talks with Koromah and his fellow junior officers who launched their coup in the early hours of Sunday.
Nigeria has troops and warships in Liberia as part of the ECOMOG regional force sent there in 1990 at the height of civil war. Some units have been backing the Sierra Leone army against the RUF.
A peace accord signed by Sankoh and Kabbah has failed to hold, and Sankoh is reported to be disillusioned with its terms.
Sierra Leone's U.N. ambassador James Jonah said Kabbah had appealed to West African countries "for help to restore democracy" which could include the use of troops.
The U.N. Security Council joined African and Western governments in condemning the coup and accompanying violence and called for "an immediate restoration of constitutional order".
A United Nations ship arrived on charter from Liberia on Tuesday ready to evacuate non-essential U.N. staff and their dependants.

The U.S. navy helicopter ship Kearsarge with 1,200 Marines headed for Sierra Leone from the waters off Zaire, where it had been on standby for a possible evacuation during the final days of Mobutu Sese Seko's rule.
"An American warship entering the waters of Sierra Leone is provocative," Sankoh told Reuters. "They should rest assured that their nationals are safe."
At least 40 people, including two Nigerian soldiers, were killed and twice that number wounded in fighting on Sunday, hospital sources said.
